newsitem.title: THAILAND: Significant Thai rate cuts only seen early-1997.
newsitem.headline: Significant Thai rate cuts only seen early-1997.

text.p: Any significant reduction in Thailand's high interest rates, after a surprise central bank call for cuts to boost the economy, is only likely early next year, bankers said on Wednesday.

Intense competition among commercial banks to attract deposits and concern about the impact of lower rates on their earnings would make it hard for them to make any meaningful rate cuts this year, the bankers told Reuters.
"The central bank's clear signal for a cut in interest rates on Tuesday will certainly put pressure on local interest rates," said Montira Utarapichat, vice president of Bank of Asia Plc.

"But any significant reduction in interest rates by commercial banks will only be seen from early next year due to the banks' concerns about (the) impact on their earnings and competition for deposits," she added.
Bank of Thailand governor Rerngchai Marakanond said on Tuesday that commercial banks should cut their lending and deposit interest rates to help boost the slowing economy.
A reduction in local interest rates would also help boost sluggish credit growth, which rose only 16 to 17 percent this year, he added.
Thailand has some of the highest interest rates in the region with the Minimum Lending Rate ranging from 13.25 percent to 13.50 percent.
The central bank has followed a tight monetary policy to combat rising inflation that was a problem early this year, but the latest inflation figures released in October showed an easing trend.
In October, Thailand's consumer price index rose 4.3 percent year-on-year, the slowest growth rate in three years, against 4.6 percent in the same month a year ago.
Thai economic growth has slowed significantly, and private analysts predict gross domestic product growth of just above 6.0 percent in 1996 from 8.6 percent in 1995.
Thai export growth has fallen sharply this year, the property sector is depressed, the current account deficit is causing concern and private investment has slowed.
Before 1995, the economy expanded at about nine percent annually for a decade.
But foreign investors have maintained an interest in the country's financial markets, the bankers said.

A clearer political picture after Sunday's general election and progress by Chavalit Yongchaiyudh in forming a coalition government have attracted foreign funds and raised liquidity in the system, they said. Chavalit heads the New Aspiration Party, which won the most parliamentary seats in the election.

"Foreigner confidence in Thai financial markets appears to be improving, as can be seen from higher liquidity and a fall in baht swap premiums," said Singha Nikornpun, director and senior treasurer at Deutsche Bank AG.
"Foreign investors realise that (the) coalition government being formed is paying much attention to economic policies that will shore up the country's sagging economy," he added.
Bank of Asia's Montira said foreign investors were still interested in Thai financial markets due to the attractive interest rates and a relatively stable currency.
High liquidity compounded by the central bank's call for lower rates should accelerate commercial bank reductions in interest rates, the bankers added.
